subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In the carbon cycle, how is carbon dioxide removed from the atmosphere?
questions.explain: Photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide from the air, using it to make glucose in plants.

questions.q: Which disease is caused by a protist spread by mosquitoes?
questions.explain: Malaria is caused by a protist, with mosquitoes acting as vectors that transfer it between people.

questions.q: Why do food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels?
options: There is not enough energy passed on to support more levels
Animals refuse to eat each other
There are not enough species on Earth
questions.explain: So little energy is passed up each level that there is not enough to support many more top consumers.

questions.q: Phagocytosis is the process by which white blood cells:
questions.explain: Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens, a non-specific form of defence.

questions.q: Which white blood cell process involves producing proteins that lock onto antigens?
questions.explain: Lymphocytes produce antibodies with a complementary shape to a pathogen's antigens, marking them for destruction.

questions.q: How does antibiotic resistance in bacteria arise and spread?
options: Random mutations make some bacteria resistant, and these survive and reproduce
Bacteria choose to become resistant when needed
Humans pass resistance directly to bacteria
questions.explain: Resistant bacteria arise by chance mutation, then survive antibiotic treatment and reproduce, spreading resistance.

questions.q: Antitoxins produced by white blood cells work by:
options: Neutralising the toxins released by pathogens
Forming a barrier on the skin
questions.explain: Antitoxins are produced by lymphocytes and counteract the harmful toxins released by pathogens such as bacteria.

questions.q: Cilia and mucus in the trachea and bronchi help defend the body by:
options: Trapping pathogens and wafting them away from the lungs
questions.explain: Mucus traps pathogens and tiny cilia sweep the mucus up away from the lungs, a non-specific defence.

questions.q: Which type of pathogen causes measles?
questions.explain: Measles is caused by a virus, which is spread by droplets from sneezes and coughs.

questions.q: What is the main role of stomach acid in defending against disease?
options: It kills pathogens in swallowed food and mucus
It traps dust in the airways
questions.explain: Hydrochloric acid in the stomach kills most pathogens that are swallowed.

questions.q: Rose black spot is caused by which type of pathogen?
questions.explain: Rose black spot is a fungal disease that produces purple/black spots on leaves and reduces plant growth.

questions.q: Which of these is a NON-specific first line of defence against pathogens?
options: The skin acting as a barrier
questions.explain: The skin is a physical barrier that is non-specific, stopping pathogens entering before the immune response.

questions.q: Gonorrhoea is a sexually transmitted disease caused by a bacterium. How can its spread be controlled?
questions.explain: Gonorrhoea is treated with antibiotics, and barrier methods such as condoms reduce its spread.

questions.q: During which stage are new drugs first tested for toxicity on cells, tissues and live animals?
questions.explain: Preclinical testing uses cells, tissues and animals before any human trials begin.

questions.q: Why can viruses NOT be treated with antibiotics?
options: Viruses are too large for antibiotics to reach
Viruses reproduce inside the body's own cells, where antibiotics cannot easily target them
Viruses are killed only by stomach acid
questions.explain: Viruses live and reproduce inside host cells, so antibiotics (which target bacterial processes) cannot kill them.

questions.q: What is herd immunity?
options: When enough people are vaccinated that a disease cannot spread easily, protecting the unvaccinated too
When antibiotics are given to a whole population
When animals become immune to human diseases
When farm herds are vaccinated together
questions.explain: If a large proportion of a population is immune, pathogens struggle to spread, so even unvaccinated people are protected.

questions.q: How do bacteria typically make us feel ill?
options: By producing toxins that damage tissues
By replacing our white blood cells
By living inside our cells and only reproducing
questions.explain: Bacteria reproduce rapidly and can release toxins that damage tissues and cause illness.

questions.q: Why are antibiotics useless against the common cold?
options: The cold virus is resistant to all drugs
Colds are caused by viruses, and antibiotics only kill bacteria
questions.explain: Antibiotics kill bacteria but cannot kill viruses, which reproduce inside the body's own cells.

questions.q: Why does a vaccinated person respond faster if they later meet the real pathogen?
options: Memory cells remain and quickly produce antibodies
questions.explain: Vaccination leaves memory cells that rapidly produce the correct antibodies on re-exposure.

questions.q: Which pathogen type causes the disease known as 'athlete's foot'?
questions.explain: Athlete's foot is a fungal skin infection that grows in warm, moist conditions between the toes.

questions.q: Where was the painkiller aspirin originally derived from?
questions.explain: Aspirin originates from a chemical found in willow bark; many drugs originally came from plants.

questions.q: A new painkiller is tested. In a clinical trial, what is the purpose of giving some patients a placebo?
options: To act as a control so the drug's real effect can be measured
To make the trial finish faster
questions.explain: A placebo acts as a control, allowing scientists to compare and see whether the drug itself has a genuine effect.
